vignette:
When Miguel Alvarez was beaten by police two years ago, he had been leaving a late client meeting during tax season, still carrying a leather portfolio and thinking about deadlines. A patrol car slowed beside him after someone reported a man “acting suspicious” near parked vehicles. He remembered trying to explain where he worked and reaching for his ID, then the abrupt escalation: being shoved against the hood, the crack of his cheekbone against metal, a knee driven into his side, the hot burst of pain along his ribs and shoulder while one officer kept shouting for him to stop resisting. What stayed with him most sharply was not only his own pain but the sight of blood running from his eyebrow onto his shirt and, in the blur beside him, another man on the sidewalk with a split lip staring helplessly at him. Since then, images of injured faces and wounded bodies have carried an immediate charge. If he notices bruises on a stranger in the grocery store or a cut on a client’s hand across his desk, he is no longer simply seeing an injury; he is back in the logic of that night, seized by the sense that damaged bodies mean someone has been overpowered and no one will help.

In the months after the assault, Miguel found that reminders of victims worked on him in the same way. News footage of someone being restrained, a story about a person hurt during an arrest, even a passing mention from a client about an injured relative could pull him toward the same thought: this happened because there is something about him that made him a target. He had come to believe he was marked in some essential way, the kind of man authority could pick out, humiliate, and harm. Those moments left him feeling apart from everyone around him, as if other people still moved through an ordinary world while he had been pushed outside it. On his worst nights, especially when pain flared again in his ribs or shoulder where he had been pinned, he found himself wondering whether his life was worth much now at all.

That belief changed how he moved through the world. Miguel, once comfortable driving to unfamiliar office parks to meet clients, now avoids new places whenever he can because he cannot relax until he has judged every entrance, hallway, and parking lot. At his downtown tax office he chooses the chair that lets him see the door, notes the back exit before he can focus on a conversation, and when he walks to the garage he checks behind him again and again for footsteps or a slow-moving car. He tells himself this is just being careful, but beneath it is a more despairing conviction: he is alone in keeping himself alive, and if something happens again no one will step in. Feeling cut off from other people and fundamentally at fault has made vigilance seem necessary, almost moral.

Over time that vigilance has tightened rather than reassured him. Because Miguel is always scanning for danger, he notices every limp, bandage, bruise, and pained expression in exaggerated detail. A client arriving with stitches over his eyebrow can derail an entire appointment; Miguel’s attention fixes on the wound, and the rest of the man’s face drops away. If his old rib pain starts while he is sitting in a conference room, the sensation quickly becomes more than pain—it becomes proof that the past is close and can happen again. He leaves restaurants after locating exits, circles unfamiliar waiting rooms with his eyes, and in that constant state of readiness he keeps stumbling into the very reminders that undo him.

Each time this happens, the meaning he gives it grows harsher. After a meeting interrupted by a client’s story about his son being assaulted, Miguel sat in his car for nearly an hour thinking that he was not like other men his age, divorced and living alone in a condo that felt more like a bunker than a home. He was certain there was something damaged in him that others could somehow detect. When he catches himself checking over his shoulder on a quiet sidewalk or mapping escape routes in a coffee shop before he can even taste his drink, he does not experience that as a symptom but as evidence that he has become the sort of person who can never rejoin ordinary life. That conclusion deepens the isolation and, at its bleakest, feeds the thought that there may be little point in continuing like this.

Miguel finally sought help after losing a longstanding client. During a routine review at the client’s small business, he became distracted by a delivery driver’s heavily bandaged forearm and then abruptly ended the meeting after noticing there was only one clear exit from the back office. The client later told him he seemed distant and unsettled. That embarrassment frightened him almost as much as the memories themselves, because his work has always been the part of life where he felt most competent. Now he comes to treatment exhausted by the effort of staying on guard and afraid of how quickly a wound, a victim’s story, or a stab of pain in his side can collapse him into the conviction that he is permanently set apart. What he hopes, cautiously, is not to feel safe all the time, but to stop living as if the next corner, the next room, or the next injured face will prove that his life ended that night.
